_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss in another section (Bernadette's refusal vs Oskar's plans to leave; Nadia's busy nights vs Oskar's quiet ones). Used by the Part 7 practice page.
title: While you were sleeping
subtitle: Four people describe what it is like to work through the night.

sections.A: Callum, 29, road maintenance worker. We resurface motorways, and the only time you can close a lane without causing chaos is between ten at night and five in the morning. It's hard, physical work, and in winter your fingers stop working by about two. The pay is noticeably better, though, because there's an extra allowance for nights, and that's what keeps most of us going. Sleeping during the day was a nightmare at first, especially in summer. In the end I fitted blackout blinds and stuck foil over the window frame, so my bedroom now looks like a spaceship, but I get seven solid hours. The worst part is missing things at my kids' school, like sports days and concerts. The best part? At the end of every shift, the whole crew goes to the same roadside café for a huge fry-up before going home.
sections.B: Nadia, 36, emergency vet. I work nights at an animal hospital, and you genuinely never know what's coming through the door. Some nights it's one cat with a sore paw and I catch up on paperwork; other nights I'll see ten serious cases back to back. During the day there are always senior colleagues around to ask, but at three in the morning it's just me and a nurse, so if a dog needs an operation, I'm the one deciding. That was terrifying in my first year. Funnily enough, I now prefer nights: no meetings, no office politics. The hardest thing is my relationship. My partner's a teacher, so we're hardly ever awake at the same time. We leave each other notes on the fridge, and some weeks that's most of our conversation. I eat terribly too, mostly biscuits from the staff room.
sections.C: Oskar, 23, museum security guard. I look after a natural history museum overnight, which sounds exciting but mostly involves walking the same corridors every hour and checking doors. I'll be honest: the first few weeks were frightening. In the dark, the stuffed bears and the giant skeleton in the main hall look very different, and I kept thinking I'd heard footsteps. Now I hardly notice them. Between my rounds, nothing happens, absolutely nothing, so I use the time to study for a law degree online. My manager doesn't mind as long as every check is done. I'll leave once I've qualified, of course; I can't imagine doing this for ever. People ask how I cope with the hours, but I've always been a night owl. I sleep from nine until four, and my body seems perfectly happy with that.
sections.D: Bernadette, 58, radio presenter. For fifteen years I've presented a phone-in programme from midnight till four. My listeners are lorry drivers, nurses on their break, new parents feeding babies, people who simply can't sleep. I've never met most of them, but I feel I know them better than some of my neighbours, and many have been calling for years. When one regular, a long-distance driver called Stan, retired last spring, half the country seemed to ring in to say goodbye. Friends assume it must be a lonely job, sitting in a studio while the city sleeps. It isn't. Two years ago the station offered me the breakfast show, which is supposedly the top job in radio, and I said no without a second thought. My children have grown up and left home, so there's nobody to complain about my strange timetable apart from the cat.

questions.question: Which person rejected an offer to work during the day?
questions.why: The station 'offered me the breakfast show… and I said no'. Oskar plans to leave, but has not been offered anything.

questions.question: Which person has to take serious decisions with no one more experienced to turn to?
questions.why: 'At three in the morning it's just me and a nurse… I'm the one deciding.'

questions.question: Which person was scared by their surroundings when they started?
questions.why: 'The first few weeks were frightening… I kept thinking I'd heard footsteps.' Nadia's fear came from decisions, not the place.

questions.question: Which person receives additional pay for the hours they work?
Which person often communicates with their partner in writing?
questions.why: 'We leave each other notes on the fridge.'

questions.question: Which person feels a strong connection with people they have never seen?
questions.why: 'I've never met most of them, but I feel I know them better than some of my neighbours.'

questions.question: Which person is using the job as a step towards a different profession?
questions.why: He studies 'for a law degree online' and will 'leave once I've qualified'.

questions.question: Which person made changes to their room so they could rest in the daytime?
questions.why: 'I fitted blackout blinds and stuck foil over the window frame.' Oskar has no trouble sleeping.

questions.question: Which person says the amount of work can be very different from one shift to the next?
questions.why: 'Some nights it's one cat… other nights I'll see ten serious cases.' At Oskar's museum 'nothing happens' between rounds.

questions.question: Which person enjoys eating with colleagues after work?
questions.why: 'The whole crew goes to the same roadside café for a huge fry-up.' Nadia eats biscuits from the staff room, which she does not enjoy.
